q: What are human rights?
What is the definition of human rights?
Where do human rights come from?
What are the basic principles of human rights?
What is the difference between human rights and civil rights?
Are human rights universal?
What are the characteristics of human rights?
a: Human rights are fundamental rights and freedoms inherent to every person by virtue of being human, regardless of nationality, ethnicity, religion, gender, or any other status — they are universal (apply everywhere), inalienable (cannot be taken away, though can be limited in specific circumstances), indivisible (all rights are equally important), and interdependent (enjoyment of one right often depends on others). The modern human rights framework was established after World War II with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR, 1948), which together with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) forms the International Bill of Human Rights. Human rights differ from civil rights in that civil rights are legal protections granted by a particular state to its citizens (such as the US Civil Rights Act), while human rights are understood as moral and legal entitlements belonging to all people under international law.

q: What is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
What does the UDHR contain?
Who wrote the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
When was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted?
Is the UDHR legally binding?
What are the main categories of rights in the UDHR?
What is the significance of Article 1 of the UDHR?
a: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on December 10, 1948, as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations — drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt with contributions from figures like René Cassin and John Peters Humphrey, it was the first global statement of the rights to which all humans are entitled. The UDHR comprises 30 articles spanning both civil and political rights (right to life, liberty, security; freedom from torture and slavery; right to fair trial; freedom of expression, thought, conscience, and religion; right to assembly and association; right to participate in government) and economic, social, and cultural rights (right to work, education, healthcare, social security, adequate standard of living, and participation in cultural life). While not a binding treaty itself, the UDHR has achieved enormous legal authority — many of its provisions are now considered customary international law, it inspired over 90 national constitutions, and it directly led to the binding ICCPR and ICESCR covenants that together make its principles legally enforceable for the 173 states that have ratified them.

q: What are examples of human rights violations?
What is genocide under international law?
What is the definition of torture?
What constitutes a crime against humanity?
What are war crimes?
How are human rights violations punished?
What is the International Criminal Court?
a: Human rights violations range from individual acts of torture, arbitrary detention, and enforced disappearance to systematic atrocities including genocide (acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group, as defined by the 1948 Genocide Convention), crimes against humanity (widespread or systematic attacks against civilian populations, including murder, enslavement, deportation, and persecution), and war crimes (serious violations of international humanitarian law in armed conflict). The International Criminal Court (ICC), established by the Rome Statute in 2002 in The Hague, prosecutes individuals for the most serious international crimes when national courts are unwilling or unable to act — with 123 member states (though notably not the US, China, Russia, or India) — and has issued indictments for leaders in conflicts including Darfur, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and Ukraine.

q: What is freedom of speech?
What are the limits of free speech?
What is freedom of religion?
What is the difference between freedom of belief and freedom of worship?
What is the separation of church and state?
How does the First Amendment protect free expression?
What is the difference between absolute and qualified free speech?
a: Freedom of speech, protected under Article 19 of the UDHR and the First Amendment of the US Constitution, guarantees the right to express opinions, ideas, and information without government censorship or fear of retaliation, but it is not absolute — limitations permitted under international law include restrictions for national security, public order, public health, and the protection of the reputations or rights of others (such as prohibitions on hate speech, incitement to violence, defamation, and child pornography). Freedom of religion, protected under Article 18 of the UDHR, encompasses the right to hold any religious belief or none at all (forum internum, which is absolute) and the right to manifest that belief through worship, observance, practice, and teaching (forum externum, which can be limited for public safety, order, health, or morals). Human rights organizations like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch monitor and report on violations of these freedoms worldwide, using methods including country reports, urgent action appeals, and advocacy to pressure governments to comply with international human rights standards.
